questions: Did this problem begin suddenly after an injury?
Did the injury involve a fall, twisting motion, or sports activity?
Did you hear or feel a pop when it happened?
Did your knee or leg look visibly deformed or out of place?
Were you unable to straighten or bend the knee afterward?
Were you unable to bear weight on that leg?
Was the kneecap visibly shifted to one side?
Did you have severe pain centered around the knee?
Did you have significant swelling that developed quickly?
Did you have an open wound near the knee?
Did you develop numbness or tingling in the foot?
Did the foot become cold, pale, or bluish?
Could you move your ankle and toes normally?
Have you dislocated or seriously injured this knee before?
Have you had surgery on this leg or knee?
Did the pain or deformity begin without any injury?
orders: Bedside neurologic and vascular examination of both lower extremities, including strength, sensation, reflexes, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, capillary refill, skin temperature, and compartment tenderness.
Manual ankle–brachial index with Doppler arterial waveforms.
Plain radiographs of the affected leg, ankle, and foot.
Duplex Doppler ultrasound of the lower-extremity arteries and veins.
MRI of the knee and lower leg.
Serum creatine kinase, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
Electromyography and nerve-conduction studies of the affected lower limb.

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Functional neurological symptom disorder (functional movement disorder) causing non-organic lower-limb weakness/abnormal posturing, without demonstrable neurologic, muscular, inflammatory, or metabolic disease

ALTERNATIVE 1: Occult intra-articular knee pathology, such as a meniscal tear causing intermittent mechanical locking

ALTERNATIVE 2: Complex regional pain syndrome without objective laboratory abnormalities

ALTERNATIVE 3: Malingering or factitious disorder
